line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 Nc3 e6 d5 d6 e4 Be7 Bd3 Nbd7 Nf3 Ng4 O-O Nge5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Be2 Bf6 f4 Ng6 Be3
teaches: Part of having a positional style is knowing when simplicity is required — when the position is rich with sharp tries, the developing move that completes your setup is often stronger than any of them, and a trade that ruins your pawns a little while opening a file for your rook is a price worth agreeing to in advance.
explains: The bishop develops to e3 and attacks the pawn on c5. The quiet move is not passive — it completes development, connects the heavy pieces, and puts a question to the queenside pawn in the same motion. The sharper pawn sacrifice was available; simplicity outranked it.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 Nc3 e6 d5 d6 e4 Be7 Bd3 Nbd7 Nf3 Ng4 O-O Nge5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Be2 Bf6 f4 Ng6 Be3 O-O dxe6 Bxe6 f5
teaches: A pawn storm earns its keep when each step lands with tempo — trade in the centre to pull a piece onto the square your pawn wants to hit, and the advance stops being a loosening gesture and becomes a forcing sequence, every move of it answered on your opponent's clock.
explains: The pawn arrives on f5 attacking the bishop on e6 and the knight on g6 at the same time — two pieces, one pawn, and only one of them can step away. The capture on e6 a move earlier is what put the bishop there, so the whole sequence was one idea: pull the piece in, then hit it and its neighbour together.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 Nc3 e6 d5 d6 e4 Be7 Bd3 Nbd7 Nf3 Ng4 O-O Nge5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Be2 Bf6 f4 Ng6 Be3 O-O dxe6 Bxe6 f5 Bd7 fxg6 fxg6 Qxd6 b6 Rad1
teaches: When a backward pawn falls, the file it lived on is the real prize — bring the rook to that file at once, because the piece that captured is strong there but exposed, and the rook behind it turns a one-move raid into permanent occupation.
explains: The queen on d6 has taken the backward pawn. The rook on d1 defends the queen along a completely open file. The whole line aimed at this pawn, and the rook move converts the raid into control of the only open file on the board.
